blocks.html: Password strength is not complexity. It is length, algorithm and work factor.
What it kills
The belief that a complicated-looking password is a strong one.
What happens

Type a password, choose how the site stored it and choose the attacker's hardware. Load a long passphrase, then switch storage from a fast hash to a slow one. The same password moves from hours to thousands of years.
What to notice

• Length matters more than substitutions.
  • The storage algorithm belongs to the site.
  • A dictionary attack with mangling rules beats clever-looking substitutions.
  • A slow hash rescues a good password, not a bad one.
Exercise
Compare a short complex password with a long passphrase under two storage schemes. Record the time-to-crack and explain which change mattered most.
Carry forward
Ask how the password is stored, not only how it looks.
Hashing is not encryption.
What it kills
The belief that a hash is a locked message you can unlock with the right key.
What happens
Encrypt a message, change one character of the key and decrypt. It fails completely, not partially. Then hash the same message and watch one changed character flip the whole fingerprint.
What to notice

• Encryption is reversible with the key.
  • A hash is a one-way fingerprint.
  • A site that can show you your old password is storing it wrongly.
  • A huge keyspace does not save a cipher whose structure leaks.
Exercise
Encrypt one sentence with two keys that differ by a single character. Compare the outputs. Then hash the same sentence twice with one character changed.
Carry forward
Ask which property the system needs: confidentiality, integrity or verification.
A good detector plus a sensible threshold still produces a queue nobody can clear.
What it kills
Base-rate neglect in security monitoring.
What happens

Ten thousand events, three intrusions. Choose the suspicion score that becomes an alert. Catch everything and the queue is thousands of alerts a day. Make the queue readable and two of the three intrusions walk past.
What to notice

• The base rate decides the false-positive volume.
  • A better detector moves the number; it does not remove the trade-off.
  • A low-and-slow intrusion can stay just above ordinary traffic.
  • Detection is a budget decision, not only a model decision.
Exercise
Find a threshold one analyst could clear in a shift. Record the intrusions caught and missed. Explain the trade-off to a manager.
Carry forward
Ask who reads the queue and what else they could be doing.
A photo is not a picture. It is a file with metadata.
What it kills
The belief that an image contains only the image.
What happens
Drop in a photo and read what the file says: camera, lens, time, often a serial number and frequently the coordinates of where you were standing.
What to notice

• Metadata can identify a place, a device and a time.
  • A serial number can link every photo from that camera.
  • Stripping metadata is a deliberate export step.
  • Use a synthetic sample on a projector; never expose a student's photo.
Exercise
Use the synthetic sample. Record three pieces of metadata a stranger could use. Then explain how you would remove them before sharing.
Carry forward
Treat a photo as a document with a hidden appendix.
Injection is a query-construction bug, not a magic word.
What it kills
The belief that SQL injection is a trick or a spell.
What happens
A login form builds a query by gluing text together. Type a quote and watch the exact character where data becomes code. The database parses the sentence it was handed and answers honestly.
What to notice

• The vulnerability is in the line that builds the query.
  • A comment marker can remove the password check.
  • Parameterised queries finish the query before the input arrives.
  • Blocking the word "OR" is not the fix.
Exercise
Run the payload, then toggle parameterisation with the same input. Explain why the safe version does not need to inspect the input.
Carry forward
Separate code from data at the point the query is built.
A firewall ruleset is a sequence, not a set.
What it kills
The belief that every rule in a firewall is simultaneously true.
What happens
Six rules, one network, five flows. Only the order changes. A leftover accept rule at position three catches everything first, and the correct-looking rules below it never run.
What to notice

• The firewall stops at the first match.
  • A rule that is never reached has no effect.
  • A catch-all left at the bottom is still a finding.
  • Specific rules usually belong before general ones.
Exercise
Move the catch-all to the bottom and check the five flows. Then explain why correct behaviour and a correct ruleset are different claims.
Carry forward
Read a ruleset in order and ask which rules can never run.
